content.overview: Section 112 BNS establishes a dedicated, codified central penal regime for Petty Organised Crime, bridging the critical statutory void between isolated street offences and syndicated cartels under Section 111. It penalizes any person who, as a member of a group or gang, either singly or jointly commits theft (broadly defined to include trick theft, vehicle/ATM theft, card skimming, cargo theft, and pickpocketing), snatching, cheating, ticket scalping, unauthorized gambling, or public examination paper leaks, imposing a mandatory minimum sentence of one year extending up to seven years, and fine.

content.study:
I. LEGISLATIVE GENESIS & THE STATUTORY GAP
Section 112 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) introduces a novel substantive offence into general Indian criminal law. It sits in Chapter VI ("Of Offences Affecting the Human Body") directly alongside Section 111 (Organised Crime) and Section 113 (Terrorist Act).
Prior to 1 July 2024, the Indian Penal Code, 1860 contained no overarching mechanism to deal with low-level organized crime networks. Street syndicates engaged in systematic mobile phone snatching, pickpocketing rings operating in metro stations, ATM card-skimming cells, ticket-scalping syndicates, and public examination paper-leak cartels were prosecuted merely as isolated, disparate offences (e.g. simple theft under old s. 379 IPC or cheating under old s. 420 IPC). Because these individual offences were bailable or carried low sentences, gang members obtained immediate bail and resumed operations, frustrating law enforcement and creating pervasive feelings of public insecurity.

In Section 112 BNS, Parliament closed this gap by creating an aggravated, non-bailable statutory category targeted at street-level organized criminality, prescribing a mandatory minimum sentence of one year extending up to seven years imprisonment, and fine.

II. STATUTORY ANATOMY & THE GROUP/GANG GATEWAY (SECTION 112(1))
Section 112(1) BNS provides:
"Whoever, being a member of a group or gang, either singly or jointly, commits any act of theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorised selling of tickets, unauthorised betting or gambling, selling of public examination question papers or any other similar criminal act, is said to commit petty organised crime."

Foundational Ingredients of Section 112(1):
1. Membership in a Group or Gang:
   - The foundational jurisdictional gateway: the accused must be a member of a "group or gang".
   - A lone, independent offender acting without gang affiliation or organizational backing cannot be charged under Section 112. An isolated opportunistic pickpocket is prosecuted under Section 303 BNS (theft), not Section 112 BNS.
   - The prosecution carries the legal burden under Section 104 BSA to establish the existence of the group or gang and prove the accused's operational membership therein.
2. Mode of Execution ("Either Singly or Jointly"):
   - Parliament deliberately enacted that the criminal act may be executed by a gang member acting alone ("singly") or in concert with others ("jointly").
   - It is not necessary that multiple gang members be physically present at the scene of the crime, provided the individual act is executed as a member of the group and serves the syndicate's enterprise.
3. The Enumerated Predicate Acts:
   - Theft (as specially defined in the Explanation);
   - Snatching (now also recognized as an aggravated offence under s. 304 BNS);
   - Cheating (under s. 318 BNS);
   - Unauthorised selling of tickets (ticket scalping and black-marketing at railway stations, concerts, sports events);
   - Unauthorised betting or gambling;
   - Selling of public examination question papers (paper leaks destabilizing educational and recruitment exams);
   - "Or any other similar criminal act": Governed by the rule of ejusdem generis, restricted to systematic, economic-gain street crimes causing public insecurity.

III. MODERN CRIMINOLOGY & DECONSTRUCTION OF THE EXPLANATION
Parliament enacted an expansive Explanation to Section 112(1) explicitly adapting criminal law to modern urban and cyber modus operandi:
"Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section 'theft' includes trick theft, theft from vehicle, dwelling house or business premises, cargo theft, pick pocketing, theft through card skimming, shoplifting and theft of Automated Teller Machine."

Key Modalities Codified:
1. Card Skimming & Cyber Theft: Encompasses the deployment of magnetic strip skimmers on ATMs or POS terminals, cloning of debit/credit cards, and credential harvesting to loot accounts.
2. Trick Theft & Distraction Thefts: Gangs using chemical distractions, tyre-puncture ruses, or fake currency drops to distract victims and steal bags.
3. Cargo Theft: Systematic hijacking or pilferage of commercial logistics, freight containers, and e-commerce transit hubs by transport gangs.
4. Public Examination Paper Leaks: Addresses the organized mafia leaking and monetizing entrance and recruitment exam question papers, addressing a major national crisis.

IV. COMPARATIVE HIERARCHY: SECTION 111 VS SECTION 112 BNS
Understanding the statutory hierarchy between Section 111 (Organised Crime) and Section 112 (Petty Organised Crime) is vital for trial strategy:
1. Prior Chargesheet Gateway: Section 111 requires proof of "continuing unlawful activity", defined as more than one chargesheet filed within the preceding ten years upon which cognizance was taken. Section 112 has NO prior chargesheet requirement; a gang member can be indicted on the very first detection of gang-backed activity.
2. Penal Severity: Section 111 prescribes death or life imprisonment (where death results) or 5 years to life, with mandatory fines of ₹5 to ₹10 lakh. Section 112 prescribes 1 year to 7 years imprisonment, and fine.
3. Target Mischief: Section 111 targets transnational cartels, extortion syndicates, and contract killers. Section 112 targets urban street gangs, paper-leak networks, card-skimming rings, and ticket scalpers.

V. FORENSIC INVESTIGATION, DIGITAL EVIDENCE & ARTICLE 20(1) TRANSITION
1. Digital Evidence under Section 63 BSA: Prosecuting card-skimming or paper-leak syndicates relies on digital seizure: skimmers, cloned cards, WhatsApp broadcasts, Telegram channels, and crypto/UPI transaction logs. All such electronic records are inadmissible unless accompanied by the mandatory certificate under Section 63(4) BSA (Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020)).
2. Establishing Gang Membership: Cannot be based on mere police suspicion or confession in custody (barred by BSA s. 23). Must be proved through call detail records, shared financial accounts, recovered gang ledgers, or co-conspirator evidence.
3. Non-Retrospectivity under Article 20(1): Section 112 BNS creates a new substantive offence carrying a mandatory minimum sentence. Under Article 20(1) of the Constitution and Section 531(2)(a) BNSS, Section 112 can ONLY be charged for acts committed on or after 1 July 2024. Charging Section 112 for pre-July 2024 thefts or cheats is unconstitutional.

sections.heading: Legislative Genesis, Purpose & The Street Syndicate Mischief
sections.body:
Section 112 BNS introduces a novel substantive offence into general Indian criminal law, sitting in Chapter VI alongside Organised Crime (s. 111) and Terrorism (s. 113).
Prior to the BNS, street syndicates engaged in pickpocketing, mobile snatching, card skimming, and paper leaks were prosecuted as isolated individual thefts or cheats under the IPC.
Because these offences were bailable or carried minor sentences, gang members obtained immediate bail and sustained chronic street operations without systemic deterrence.
Section 112 establishes an aggravated, unified penal offence for petty organized crime, prescribing a mandatory minimum sentence of one year extending up to seven years, and fine.

sections.heading: Statutory Anatomy: The Group/Gang Gateway & Enumerated Predicate Acts
sections.body:
The Gateway Threshold: The accused must commit the act as a "member of a group or gang". Lone, unorganized offenders acting independently cannot be charged under Section 112.
Execution Flexibility: The offence may be committed "either singly or jointly"; a single member operating on the street is liable if acting on behalf of or as part of the gang.
Enumerated Predicate Acts: Covers theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorised selling of tickets (scalping), unauthorised betting/gambling, selling of public examination question papers, and similar acts.
The omnibus phrase "any other similar criminal act" is governed by ejusdem generis, restricted to systematic, economic-gain street crimes causing public insecurity.

sections.heading: The Expanded Definition of Theft under the Explanation
sections.body:
The Explanation to Section 112(1) codifies modern urban and digital criminal modalities within the definition of theft.
Codified forms include: trick theft (con games), theft from vehicle/dwelling, cargo theft (freight and logistics hijacking), and pickpocketing.
Cyber and financial modalities: explicitly covers "theft through card skimming" (cloning ATM/POS magnetic strips) and physical or electronic "theft of Automated Teller Machine".
Paper Leaks: Selling or distributing public examination question papers is directly criminalized under Section 112(1), establishing severe criminal deterrence against recruitment syndicates.

sections.heading: Statutory Hierarchy: Section 111 (Organised Crime) vs Section 112 (Petty Organised Crime)
sections.body:
Section 111 BNS requires "continuing unlawful activity" with more than one prior chargesheet filed within 10 years and court cognizance; Section 112 has NO prior chargesheet requirement.
Penal hierarchy: Section 111 carries death or life imprisonment (and ₹5-10 lakh fine); Section 112 carries 1 to 7 years imprisonment and fine.
Scale of enterprise: Section 111 targets major syndicates, extortion rings, and contract killers; Section 112 targets street-level gangs, paper-leak brokers, and digital skimming cells.
Charging Section 111 for petty street crimes is an abuse of process; Section 112 provides the tailored statutory vehicle.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Proof (BSA ss. 63, 104), Digital Forensics & Article 20(1) Non-Retrospectivity
sections.body:
Proof of Gang Membership: Under BSA Section 104, the prosecution must independently prove gang affiliation through CDRs, shared accounts, or recovery of syndicate ledgers; confession in custody is inadmissible under BSA s. 23.
Digital Forensics under Section 63 BSA: Seizure of skimming hardware, cloned cards, Telegram paper-leak channels, and transaction logs must satisfy Section 63(4) certification.
Article 20(1) Non-Retrospectivity: Section 112 creates a new substantive offence and cannot be applied retrospectively to acts committed prior to 1 July 2024.
Trial Strategy: Defence counsel must attack the "group or gang" nexus to reduce the charge from Section 112 BNS to simple theft or bailable IPC/BNS provisions.

examples.title: Application of Section 112 — ATM Card-Skimming Gang Member Caught Singly
examples.body: Accused A is arrested inside an ATM kiosk in possession of a magnetic strip skimming device, a micro-pinhole camera, and 15 cloned white plastic cards. Forensic examination of A’s mobile phone reveals encrypted group chats with a known card-cloning gang allocating specific ATM kiosks across the city and distributing cloned data for cash withdrawals. Although A was physically alone at the kiosk, A acted as an active member of the card-skimming gang committing theft through card skimming. The act satisfies Section 112(1) BNS read with the Explanation, subjecting A to imprisonment from one to seven years under Section 112(2) BNS.

examples.title: Section 112 Indictment Quashed — Failure to Prove Group or Gang Membership
examples.body: College student S is apprehended outside a cricket stadium selling three extra admission tickets at double the printed face value. The police register an FIR under Section 112 BNS for petty organised crime (unauthorised selling of tickets). At the discharge stage under Section 250 BNSS, counsel demonstrates that S is a solitary individual who had purchased tickets for friends who cancelled, and that S has zero association with any scalping syndicate, gang, or organized network. The court discharges S under Section 112 BNS: Section 112 requires membership in a "group or gang"; solitary unorganized ticket reselling cannot be converted into petty organized crime.

hypotheticals.question: As Senior Counsel, analyse whether an indictment under Section 112 BNS is sustainable against R, and what evidentiary burdens the prosecution must discharge under BSA Section 104 and Section 63.
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. The Predicate Offence: The selling of public examination question papers is expressly codified as a predicate act of petty organised crime under Section 112(1) BNS. R accepted ₹50,000 per student in exchange for circulating the leaked question paper, satisfying the predicate commercial actus reus.
2. The Group/Gang Membership Gateway:
   - Under Section 112(1) BNS, the prosecution must prove that R committed the act "being a member of a group or gang, either singly or jointly".
   - Membership in a gang does not require a formal written constitution; it requires proof of operational affiliation, coordination, or shared commercial purpose with the leak network.
   - R’s systematic monetization of the leaked paper by acting as a distribution conduit between the upstream leak syndicate and candidate-buyers satisfies the threshold of operational membership.
   - Under Section 112(1), R may operate "singly" on the ground while remaining a member of the wider distribution group.
3. Evidentiary Scrutiny under Section 63 BSA:
   - The entire prosecution rests on the Telegram chat logs, digital PDFs, and UPI payments.
   - Under Section 63(4) BSA, the prosecution must produce the original devices or valid cryptographic hash certificates proving the integrity of the seized digital records. Failure to furnish the Section 63 certificate is fatal to the prosecution.

distinctions.title: Section 111 BNS (Organised Crime) vs Section 112 BNS (Petty Organised Crime)

rows.left: Requires "continuing unlawful activity" (more than one chargesheet within 10 years and court cognizance)
rows.right: No prior chargesheet requirement; applies to first detected gang-backed street crime

rows.left: Death or imprisonment for life (where death results) or 5 years to life; fine ₹5 to ₹10 lakh
rows.right: Imprisonment not less than 1 year extending up to 7 years, and fine

rows.left: Major syndicates: extortion, contract killing, trafficking, high-value financial scams
rows.right: Street syndicates: snatching, pickpocketing, card skimming, ticket scalping, paper leaks

rows.left: Special presumption under s. 111(7) for unaccounted assets held for syndicate
rows.right: Governed by general BSA burden rules without special asset presumptions

distinctions.title: Section 112 BNS (Petty Organised Crime) vs Section 303 BNS (Simple Theft)

rows.left: Offender must be a member of an organized group or gang
rows.right: Individual offender acting independently without any gang nexus

rows.left: Mandatory minimum sentence of 1 year, extending up to 7 years
rows.right: Imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both (community service for first offence < ₹5,000)

rows.left: Strictly non-bailable under the First Schedule of BNSS
rows.right: Bailable or subject to standard First Schedule rules

misconceptions.trap: Any individual who commits pickpocketing or snatching is automatically guilty of Section 112 BNS.
misconceptions.correction: Section 112 BNS explicitly requires that the accused must be a "member of a group or gang". An isolated individual who steals or snatches without gang membership is prosecuted under Section 303 (theft) or Section 304 (snatching) BNS, not Section 112 BNS.

misconceptions.trap: Section 112 BNS requires the prosecution to prove prior chargesheets within the last ten years like Section 111.
misconceptions.correction: The requirement of more than one chargesheet within ten years is specific to Section 111 BNS (Organised Crime). Section 112 BNS has no such prior-chargesheet prerequisite; proof of present gang membership and commission of an enumerated act suffices.

misconceptions.trap: Section 112 BNS can be applied retrospectively to street thefts committed before 1 July 2024.
misconceptions.correction: Section 112 is a new substantive penal offence created by Parliament in 2023. Under Article 20(1) of the Constitution and Section 531(2)(a) BNSS, it applies strictly to criminal acts committed on or after 1 July 2024.

cases.name: Mahipal Singh v. Central Bureau of Investigation
cases.holding: Established that organized crime provisions cannot be invoked against an accused in an isolated individual capacity; the prosecution must establish a direct organic nexus connecting the accused to the criminal syndicate.
cases.relevance: Foundational authority applied mutatis mutandis to enforce the "group or gang" gateway under Section 112 BNS.

cases.name: Kavitha Lankesh v. State of Karnataka
cases.holding: Held that it is not necessary that every individual member of an organized group must have prior cases registered against them; if the group’s organized nature is proved, any member facilitating or executing acts on its behalf is liable under organized crime law.
cases.relevance: Authoritative precedent supporting Section 112(1) prosecution of individual gang members executing street operations singly.

cases.name: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
cases.holding: Held that compliance with the statutory certificate for electronic records is mandatory and an indispensable condition precedent for the admissibility of digital evidence.
cases.relevance: Mandatory benchmark for all card skimming, paper leak, and cyber evidence tendered under Section 112 BNS.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Prepare an IRAC Legal Case Brief on Section 112 BNS (Petty Organised Crime), analyzing the group/gang gateway, the Explanation deconstructing theft and card skimming, and the contrast with Section 111 BNS.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & JURISDICTIONAL THRESHOLD
Whether an indictment under Section 112 BNS for petty organised crime is sustainable against an accused arrested for theft, card skimming, snatching, or paper leaks, and whether the prosecution has established the jurisdictional gateway of "group or gang" membership. Forum: Magistrate of the First Class / Court of Session under the First Schedule of BNSS.

II. GOVERNING RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
1. The Statutory Gateway: Section 112(1) BNS requires that the offender, being a member of a group or gang, either singly or jointly commits any act of theft, snatching, cheating, ticket scalping, unauthorized gambling, paper leaks, or similar acts.
2. The Expanded Explanation: Deems trick theft, cargo theft, pickpocketing, card skimming, shoplifting, and ATM theft as qualifying predicate acts.
3. Sentence: Mandatory minimum 1 year extending up to 7 years imprisonment, and fine (s. 112(2)).
4. Distinction from Section 111: No requirement of prior chargesheets within 10 years; targets street syndicates rather than major cartels.

III. APPLICATION TO FACTUAL DISPUTE
- Step 1: Verify FIR date. Offence must be committed on or after 1 July 2024 to satisfy Article 20(1).
- Step 2: Test gang membership under BSA Section 104. If the accused acted alone without proof of gang affiliation, move for alteration of charge to simple theft (s. 303) or snatching (s. 304).
- Step 3: For digital crimes (skimming / paper leaks), scrutinize Section 63(4) BSA compliance for seized hardware and messaging logs.

IV. CONCLUSION & OPERATIVE ADVICE
Advise defence counsel to target the missing "gang" element at the discharge stage under Section 250 BNSS. If the prosecution fails to produce evidence of shared revenue, gang hierarchy, or coordinated operations, seek discharge under Section 112 BNS and alteration to bailable or lesser individual offences.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Draft comprehensive Written Submissions seeking discharge under Section 250 BNSS of an accused improperly indicted under Section 112 BNS for a solitary, unorganized street dispute.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
IN THE COURT OF THE JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE OF THE FIRST CLASS AT [JURISDICTION]
CRIMINAL CASE NO. [____] OF 202[ ]
IN THE MATTER OF:
STATE                                                       ... PROSECUTION
VERSUS
ACCUSED [NAME]                                              ... ACCUSED

WRITTEN SUBMISSIONS ON BEHALF OF THE ACCUSED PRAYING FOR DISCHARGE UNDER SECTION 250 BNSS FROM CHARGES UNDER SECTION 112 BNS

MOST RESPECTFULLY SHOWETH:

I. PRELIMINARY STATEMENT & PROCEDURAL PROVENANCE
1. The Accused stands charged under Section 112 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), for allegedly committing petty organised crime.
2. The prosecution allegation is that the Accused snatched a mobile phone from a commuter at a bus terminal.

II. TOTAL ABSENCE OF THE ESSENTIAL INGREDIENT OF "GROUP OR GANG"
3. Section 112(1) BNS explicitly opens with the mandatory jurisdictional condition:
   "Whoever, being a member of a group or gang, either singly or jointly..."
4. The Supreme Court in Mahipal Singh v. CBI (2014) 11 SCC 282 authoritatively established that penal provisions targeting organized syndicates cannot be invoked against an accused in an isolated individual capacity.
5. In the entire chargesheet filed under Section 193 BNSS, the prosecution has:
   - Named no co-accused, gang leader, or syndicate;
   - Disclosed no prior criminal history or gang affiliation;
   - Produced zero Call Detail Records (CDRs) or financial links showing association with any crime network.
6. A solitary, independent thief who acts opportunistically cannot be roped into Section 112 BNS. The offence, at highest, constitutes individual snatching under Section 304 BNS.

III. STATUTORY MISUSE & INADMISSIBILITY UNDER SECTION 63 BSA
7. Converting ordinary street offences into Section 112 BNS without proof of gang membership is an abuse of process designed solely to defeat bail.
8. Furthermore, the purported CCTV footage relied upon by the police has not been certified under Section 63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, and is legally inadmissible under Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020) 7 SCC 1.

PRAYER
Wherefore, in light of the above facts, statutory scheme, and binding authorities, it is respectfully prayed that this Hon’ble Court may graciously be pleased to:
(a) Discharge the Accused under Section 250 BNSS of charges under Section 112 BNS; and
(b) Alter the charge, if any, to Section 304 BNS and grant bail to the Accused.

FILED BY:
[COUNSEL FOR THE ACCUSED]
ADVOCATE

examTips: Always identify the "member of a group or gang" threshold as the indispensable gateway for Section 112 BNS.

Contrast Section 112 (no prior chargesheet requirement) with Section 111 (requires multiple prior chargesheets in 10 years).
Emphasize Article 20(1) non-retrospectivity: Section 112 applies only to offences committed on or after 1 July 2024.
revisionPoints: BNS s. 112 = Petty organised crime: member of group/gang committing theft, snatching, skimming, paper leaks, scalping.
Punishment: 1 to 7 years imprisonment + fine (mandatory minimum 1 year).
Explanation: Includes trick theft, card skimming, ATM theft, cargo theft, pickpocketing.
